title: Noah builds (Genesis 6:5–22)
hook: in a violent world, one man builds a boat on dry land

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nod, the land of wandering: Cain's wife, the questions kids ask, and Enoch, who walked with God. Your line: good questions are welcome here. Today ends the week.

Somewhere right now, someone is working on a thing nobody around them believes in. A novel in a drawer. A garden in a vacant lot. A recovery, ninety days in. Friends ask, gently, how long you're going to keep at that. In Genesis, the world after the garden goes from bad to worse. One murder becomes many. And in the middle of it, one man is handed a set of building plans for something enormous, for a disaster nobody can see coming.
screen: `A THING NOBODY BELIEVES IN.` → `THE WORLD GOES FROM BAD TO WORSE.` → `ONE MAN, A SET OF PLANS.`

segments.voice: Chapter six opens with grief. God sees that the wickedness of humans is great, and the text says it grieved him at his heart. Then the diagnosis, in the King James Bible: "the earth was filled with violence." The Hebrew word for violence there is chamas: brutality, wrong done to others. But one verse cuts across the darkness: "But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD." Noah, the text says, was a just man, and he walked with God, the same phrase used for Enoch yesterday. So God gives him plans. An ark of gopher wood, nobody's quite sure what tree that is, three hundred cubits long, fifty wide, thirty high. A building, lying on its side. And the Hebrew word for ark, tevah, isn't the usual word for a ship. It means something like a box, a chest. The same word turns up again in Exodus, for the little basket of reeds that carries baby Moses on the Nile. Two boxes, one huge and one tiny, each carrying the future through deadly water. Popular retellings add crowds of neighbors mocking him. Genesis doesn't. A later New Testament letter calls Noah a preacher of righteousness, but the chapter itself gives him no lines at all. Noah never says a word until after the flood. What it records is this: "Thus did Noah; according to all that God commanded him, so did he." That's the week's last step: from a person alone, a twisting question, a call to come out, clothes for the road, a brother to keep, a slow walk, to a man who just builds.
screen: `THE EARTH FILLED WITH VIOLENCE.` · `NOAH FOUND GRACE.` · `TEVAH: A BOX, LIKE MOSES'S BASKET.` · `NO LINES, JUST BUILDING.` · then, large: `THUS DID NOAH.`

segments.voice: Think of something you're building that not everyone believes in, a habit, a project, a relationship, and picture it as it is: half-finished, a frame of boards on dry land, with the doubts around it. Then picture just the next plank, one small thing. If you pray, you can offer it to God.
Ark. Tevah in Hebrew, a box or chest. The huge boat Noah builds, and the same word as the tiny basket that carries baby Moses.
Your line: build anyway. Thus did Noah, without a word. Day three hundred forty-three, and a week complete.

howItsDone: Christians often see Noah as a model of faithful obedience, and early Christian writers used the ark as a picture of the church and of baptism, carrying people safely through the water.

chat.says: What does Noah actually say when God hands him the plans for the ark?
options: Nothing. Genesis gives him no lines; he does all God commanded.
He asks God how long the rain will last, then gets to work.
He pleads for his neighbors, the way Abraham later pleads for a city.
chat.meaning: Noah never says a word until after the flood. The text records only this: thus did Noah; according to all that God commanded him, so did he.

gopher wood.meaning: the ark's wood; nobody's quite sure what tree it is

cubits.meaning: an ancient measure of length used for the ark
